opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is that what we ultimately care about is how AI systems are going to affect the world, and a lot of that comes down to whether they can actually do the kinds of things people get paid to do. Benchmarks have historically been built around tasks that are convenient to score: multiple-choice questions, short coding puzzles, things with a clean right answer. Those are useful, but there's often a big gap between doing well on them and being able to do messy, open-ended, economically valuable work.

When you draw tasks from real work, like actual software engineering problems or research tasks that someone had to do, a few things improve. First, the task distribution is closer to what we care about, so performance tells you more about real-world impact. Second, real tasks have a lot of implicit structure that's hard to design artificially. There's ambiguity, you have to figure out what's being asked, there are long dependencies, you have to recover from mistakes. Those are often where current systems fall down, and synthetic benchmarks tend to sand those features off.

Third, it gives you a natural way to anchor difficulty. If you know how long a task takes a skilled human, you can say something like "this model can reliably do tasks that take a person about an hour," which is much more interpretable to policymakers or anyone else than "it scored 73% on benchmark X." And you can track that over time and look at trends.

It's not free. Real tasks are expensive to collect, harder to score, and there are contamination and representativeness worries. But if the goal is to forecast things like automation of AI research or other high-stakes capabilities, I think you really want your measurements grounded in the actual work, not a proxy that might saturate long before the real capability shows up.

r001.rationale: The response says real-work tasks better match what matters and expose ambiguity and other challenges, but it does not say representativeness matters because we do not fully understand the conditions governing AI success or failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the basic reason is that the thing we actually care about is whether these systems can do the work that people get paid to do, or that matters for the world in some concrete way. And a lot of benchmarks don't really measure that. They measure something that's correlated with it, maybe, like performance on exam questions or on toy coding puzzles, but the gap between "can solve a LeetCode problem" and "can do the job of a software engineer for a week" is enormous, and it's exactly the gap that we're most uncertain about.

So when you draw tasks from real work, a few things happen. One is that you get the messiness for free. Real tasks have ambiguous specifications, they have context you have to go find, they have parts that are tedious and parts that require judgment, and you don't have to artificially construct that because it's just there. If you try to write a hard task from scratch, you tend to write something that's hard in the way you expect, and the models often turn out to be good at precisely that kind of difficulty and bad at something you didn't think to include.

The second thing is that it gives you a much more interpretable number. If I tell you a model scores 60% on some abstract reasoning benchmark, it's genuinely unclear what that means for anything. If I tell you it completed a task that would take a professional researcher four hours and it did it successfully, that's a statement that connects to the actual world. You can start to reason about what that implies for labor, for research acceleration, for safety, whatever you're interested in.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that real tasks are a kind of validation of the whole measurement. When we built GPQA, for instance, we had domain experts write the questions and we had other experts try to answer them, and part of the point was to establish that these were things people with real expertise could do and people without it couldn't. That's a kind of grounding. With work-derived tasks you get grounding in a similar way: you know a human did this, you know roughly how long it took, you know what "done" looked like. So you're not just measuring the model against itself or against some made-up rubric.

The honest caveat is that it's expensive and slow. Collecting real tasks, getting them into a form where you can actually run a model on them, building the grading, all of that takes a lot of effort per task compared to scraping questions off the internet. So you end up with smaller evaluations and you have to be careful about what you can conclude. But I'd rather have fifty tasks that mean something than fifty thousand that don't.

r001.rationale: The response says the gap between benchmark performance and doing real jobs is what we are most uncertain about, and explains that work-derived tasks capture messy, hard-to-predict features of real work. This communicates why evaluating on representative tasks matters under uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that we care about what these systems can actually do in the world, and tasks drawn from real work give us a more direct way to measure that. If a model does well on a benchmark, you still have to ask how that translates into its ability to do something useful. Starting with real work makes that connection clearer.

It also helps capture things that are easy to leave out when you construct a benchmark: figuring out what the problem is, working with incomplete information, and checking whether the result actually meets someone’s needs. A system might be very good at answering a neatly specified question and still struggle with the larger task that question came from.

Of course, you still have to be careful about which work you sample and how you judge success. Making a task realistic doesn’t automatically make it a good evaluation. But it gives you a useful starting point for interpreting what a score means.

r001.rationale: The response says real-work tasks make evaluation more directly relevant and capture broader task demands, but it does not state that representativeness matters because we do not fully understand the conditions governing AI systems’ success or failure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we care about what these systems can actually do in the world, and tasks drawn from real work give us a more direct way to measure that. If a model does well on a task that someone genuinely needed to solve, that’s evidence of a useful capability, rather than just an ability to answer questions in a particular benchmark format.

Real work also brings in things that are easy to leave out when you design an evaluation from scratch. The problem might be underspecified, you might need to find the relevant information, and you might have to check whether your solution actually works. Those can be substantial parts of the difficulty.

That doesn’t mean real-world tasks are automatically good evaluations. You still need to think carefully about whether they’re representative and how you’re grading them. But they help anchor the evaluation to the thing we ultimately want to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations should be representative, but does not connect that to limited understanding of the conditions governing AI systems’ success or failure.
